e-5245.knowledge_point: Equating Real and Imaginary Parts of a Complex Number to Solve For an Unknown Quantity
e-5245.problem: Given that $3+2\textrm{i} = a + \textrm{i}b,$ calculate the value of $a$ and the value of $b.$
e-5245.worked_solution:
First, we equate the real parts:

$$
3 = a
$$

Then, we equate the imaginary parts:

$$
2 = b
$$

Therefore, $a=3$ and $b=2.$

e-5261.knowledge_point: Solving for Unknowns By Computing a Product and Equating Real and Imaginary Parts
e-5261.worked_solution:
First, we multiply both sides of the equation by $1+2\textrm{i}$ to get rid of the fraction and isolate the variables:

$$
\begin{aligned}2-3\text{i} & =\frac{p-2q\text{i}}{1+2\text{i}} \\ (2-3\text{i})(1+2\text{i}) & =p-2q\text{i} \\ 2+4\text{i}-3\text{i}-6{\text{i}}^{2} & =p-2q\text{i} \\ 2+\text{i}-6(-1) & =p-2q\text{i} \\ 8+\text{i} & =p-2q\text{i}\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we can equate the real parts and the imaginary parts separately.

- Equating the real parts, we get

$$
8 = p.
$$

- Equating the imaginary parts, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}1 & =-2q \\ q & =-\frac{1}{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, $p=8$ and $q = -\dfrac{1}{2}.$

e-5293.knowledge_point: Solving for Unknowns By Computing a Quotient and Equating Real and Imaginary Parts
e-5293.worked_solution:
First, we divide both sides of the equation by $1+\textrm{i}$ to isolate the variables:

$$
\begin{aligned}3+5\text{i} & =(p+\text{i}q)(1+\text{i}) \\ \frac{3+5\text{i}}{1+\text{i}} & =p+\text{i}q\end{aligned}
$$

Now, to simplify the fraction on the left-hand side, we multiply the numerator and denominator by the conjugate of the denominator:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{(3+5\text{i})(1-\text{i})}{(1+\text{i})(1-\text{i})} & =p+\text{i}q \\ \frac{3-3\text{i}+5\text{i}-5{\text{i}}^{2}}{{1}^{2}-{\text{i}}^{2}} & =p+\text{i}q \\ \frac{3+2\text{i}-5(-1)}{1-(-1)} & =p+\text{i}q \\ \frac{8+2\text{i}}{2} & =p+\text{i}q \\ 4+\text{i} & =p+\text{i}q\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we can equate the real parts and the imaginary parts separately.

- Equating the real parts, we get $4=p.$

- Equating the imaginary parts, we get $1=q.$

Therefore, $p=4$ and $q=1.$

after.worked_solution:
First, we equate the real parts:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{3}{4} & =a\end{aligned}
$$

Then, we equate the imaginary parts:

$$
\begin{aligned}\sqrt{3} & =b\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, $a=\frac{3}{4}$ and $b=\sqrt{3}.$

content.problem: Given that $\frac{3}{4}+\sqrt{3}\text{i}=a+b\text{i}$, calculate the value of $a$ and the value of $b.$
content.worked_solution:
First, we equate the real parts:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{3}{4} & =a\end{aligned}
$$

Then, we equate the imaginary parts:

$$
\begin{aligned}\sqrt{3} & =b\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, $a=\frac{3}{4}$ and $b=\sqrt{3}.$

$$
\begin{aligned}\sqrt{3} & =a\end{aligned}

$$
\begin{aligned}-2 & =b\end{aligned}
$$

$$

$$

Now, we can equate the real parts and the imaginary parts separately.

- Equating the real parts, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}3p & =8 \\ p & =\frac{8}{3}.\end{aligned}
$$

$$
\begin{aligned}2q & =1 \\ q & =\frac{1}{2}.\end{aligned}

$$
15=p.
$$

$$
\begin{aligned}16 & =q.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, $p=15$ and $q=16.$

a

decision.explanation: Multiply by 2-i: p+iq=(6+13i)(2-i)/5=(25+20i)/5=5+4i. Equating parts gives p=5 and q=4.

after.worked_solution:
First, we multiply both sides of the equation by $2-\text{i}$ to get rid of the fraction and isolate the variables:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{6+13\text{i}}{5} & =\frac{p+\text{i}q}{2-\text{i}} \\ \frac{1}{5}(6+13\text{i})(2-\text{i}) & =p+\text{i}q \\ \frac{1}{5}(12-6\text{i}+26\text{i}-13{\text{i}}^{2}) & =p+\text{i}q \\ \frac{1}{5}(12+13+20\text{i}) & =p+\text{i}q \\ \frac{1}{5}(25+20\text{i}) & =p+\text{i}q \\ 5+4\text{i} & =p+\text{i}q\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we can equate the real parts and the imaginary parts separately.

- Equating the real parts, we get

$$
5=p.
$$

- Equating the imaginary parts, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}4 & =q.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, $p=5$ and $q=4.$

Question 8

Given that 6+13i5=p+iq2−i, calculate p and q.

a
p=25, q=45
b
p=1, q=−35
c
p=−4, q=−3
d
p=15, q=−35
e
p=5, q=4
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

First, we multiply both sides of the equation by 2−i to get rid of the fraction and isolate the variables: 6+13i5=p+iq2−i15(6+13i)(2−i)=p+iq15(12−6i+26i−13i2)=p+iq15(12+13+20i)=p+iq15(25+20i)=p+iq5+4i=p+iq

Now, we can equate the real parts and the imaginary parts separately.

  • Equating the real parts, we get 5=p.

  • Equating the imaginary parts, we get 4=q.

Therefore, p=5 and q=4.

content.worked_solution:
First, we multiply both sides of the equation by $2-\text{i}$ to get rid of the fraction and isolate the variables:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{6+13\text{i}}{5} & =\frac{p+\text{i}q}{2-\text{i}} \\ \frac{1}{5}(6+13\text{i})(2-\text{i}) & =p+\text{i}q \\ \frac{1}{5}(12-6\text{i}+26\text{i}-13{\text{i}}^{2}) & =p+\text{i}q \\ \frac{1}{5}(12+13+20\text{i}) & =p+\text{i}q \\ \frac{1}{5}(25+20\text{i}) & =p+\text{i}q \\ 5+4\text{i} & =p+\text{i}q\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we can equate the real parts and the imaginary parts separately.

- Equating the real parts, we get

$$
5=p.
$$

- Equating the imaginary parts, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}4 & =q.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, $p=5$ and $q=4.$

$$

Now, we can equate the real parts and the imaginary parts separately.

- Equating the real parts, we get

$$
4=p.
$$

$$
\begin{aligned}-6 & =q.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, $p=4$ and $q=-6.$

Question 9

Given that −3−2i=p+iq2i, calculate p and q.

a
p=−6, q=−4
b
p=6, q=−4
c
p=−4, q=−6
d
p=4, q=−6
e
p=2, q=−3
Submit
Incorrect
EXPLANATION

First, we multiply both sides of the equation by 2i to get rid of the fraction and isolate the variables:

−3−2i=p+iq2i2i(−3−2i)=p+iq−6i−4i2=p+iq4−6i=p+iq

Now, we can equate the real parts and the imaginary parts separately.

  • Equating the real parts, we get 4=p.

  • Equating the imaginary parts, we get −6=q.

Therefore, p=4 and q=−6.

content.worked_solution:
First, we multiply both sides of the equation by $2\text{i}$ to get rid of the fraction and isolate the variables:

$$
\begin{aligned}-3-2\text{i} & =\frac{p+\text{i}q}{2\text{i}} \\ 2\text{i}(-3-2\text{i}) & =p+\text{i}q \\ -6\text{i}-4{\text{i}}^{2} & =p+\text{i}q \\ 4-6\text{i} & =p+\text{i}q\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we can equate the real parts and the imaginary parts separately.

- Equating the real parts, we get

$$
4=p.
$$

- Equating the imaginary parts, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}-6 & =q.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, $p=4$ and $q=-6.$

after.worked_solution:

$$
\begin{aligned}-4+\text{i} & =\frac{p+\text{i}q}{2\text{i}} \\ (-4+\text{i})(2\text{i}) & =p+\text{i}q \\ -8\text{i}+2{\text{i}}^{2} & =p+\text{i}q \\ -2-8\text{i} & =p+\text{i}q\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we can equate the real parts and the imaginary parts separately.

- Equating the real parts, we get

$$
-2=p.
$$

- Equating the imaginary parts, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}-8 & =q.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, $p=-2$ and $q=-8.$

Question 10

Given that −4+i=p+iq2i, calculate p and q.

a
 p=−2,q=3
b
 p=−1,q=4
c
 p=−1,q=−4
d
 p=−2,q=−8
e
 p=−4,q=2
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

First, we multiply both sides of the equation by 2i to get rid of the fraction and isolate the variables: −4+i=p+iq2i(−4+i)(2i)=p+iq−8i+2i2=p+iq−2−8i=p+iq

Now, we can equate the real parts and the imaginary parts separately.

  • Equating the real parts, we get −2=p.

  • Equating the imaginary parts, we get −8=q.

Therefore, p=−2 and q=−8.

content.knowledge_point: Solving for Unknowns By Computing a Product and Equating Real and Imaginary Parts
content.worked_solution:
First, we multiply both sides of the equation by $2\text{i}$ to get rid of the fraction and isolate the variables:

$$
\begin{aligned}-4+\text{i} & =\frac{p+\text{i}q}{2\text{i}} \\ (-4+\text{i})(2\text{i}) & =p+\text{i}q \\ -8\text{i}+2{\text{i}}^{2} & =p+\text{i}q \\ -2-8\text{i} & =p+\text{i}q\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we can equate the real parts and the imaginary parts separately.

- Equating the real parts, we get

$$
-2=p.
$$

- Equating the imaginary parts, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}-8 & =q.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, $p=-2$ and $q=-8.$

decision.explanation: Divide by 3+2i and multiply by its conjugate: p+iq=(5-i)(3-2i)/13=(13-13i)/13=1-i. Thus p=1 and q=-1.

after.name: Question 11
after.worked_solution:
First, we divide both sides of the equation by $3+2\text{i}$ to isolate the variables:

$$
\begin{aligned}5-\text{i} & =(p+\text{i}q)(3+2\text{i}) \\ \frac{5-\text{i}}{3+2\text{i}} & =p+\text{i}q\end{aligned}
$$

Now, to simplify the fraction on the left-hand side, we multiply the numerator and denominator by the conjugate of the denominator:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{(5-\text{i})(3-2\text{i})}{(3+2\text{i})(3-2\text{i})} & =p+\text{i}q \\ \frac{15-3\text{i}-10\text{i}+2{\text{i}}^{2}}{{3}^{2}-(2\text{i})^{2}} & =p+\text{i}q \\ \frac{13-13\text{i}}{9+4} & =p+\text{i}q \\ \frac{13-13\text{i}}{13} & =p+\text{i}q \\ 1-\text{i} & =p+\text{i}q\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we can equate the real parts and the imaginary parts separately.

- Equating the real parts, we get $1=p.$

- Equating the imaginary parts, we get $-1=q.$

Question 11

Given that 5−i=(p+iq)(3+2i), calculate p and q.

a
p=−3, q=−3
b
p=−1, q=−1
c
p=32, q=−32
d
p=2, q=−3
e
p=1, q=−1
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

First, we divide both sides of the equation by 3+2i to isolate the variables:

5−i=(p+iq)(3+2i)5−i3+2i=p+iq

Now, to simplify the fraction on the left-hand side, we multiply the numerator and denominator by the conjugate of the denominator:

(5−i)(3−2i)(3+2i)(3−2i)=p+iq15−3i−10i+2i232−(2i)2=p+iq13−13i9+4=p+iq13−13i13=p+iq1−i=p+iq

Now, we can equate the real parts and the imaginary parts separately.

  • Equating the real parts, we get 1=p.

  • Equating the imaginary parts, we get −1=q.

Therefore, p=1 and q=−1.

after.worked_solution:
First, we divide both sides of the equation by $3+\text{i}$ to isolate the variables:

$$
\begin{aligned}5 & =(p+q\text{i})(3+\text{i}) \\ \frac{5}{3+\text{i}} & =p+q\text{i}\end{aligned}
$$

Now, to simplify the fraction on the left-hand side, we multiply the numerator and denominator by the conjugate of the denominator:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{(5)(3-\text{i})}{(3+\text{i})(3-\text{i})} & =p+q\text{i} \\ \frac{15-5\text{i}}{{3}^{2}-(\text{i})^{2}} & =p+q\text{i} \\ \frac{15-5\text{i}}{9+1} & =p+q\text{i} \\ \frac{15-5\text{i}}{10} & =p+q\text{i} \\ \frac{3}{2}-\frac{1}{2}\text{i} & =p+q\text{i}\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we can equate the real parts and the imaginary parts separately.

- Equating the real parts, we get $\frac{3}{2}=p.$

- Equating the imaginary parts, we get $-\frac{1}{2}=q.$

Therefore, $p=\frac{3}{2}$ and $q=-\frac{1}{2}.$
